query: TC4 (Ti6Al4V) is an α + β dual-phase alloy with low hardness and poor friction and wear properties under extreme-service and high-contact-stress conditions. Earlier studies explored redesigning the bulk alloy, which risks compromising its original advantages, and several surface-modification approaches. Traditional thermal spraying and thermal plating produced weak coatings with poor substrate bonding; composite coatings suffered from uneven constituent dispersion and weak interfaces; and laser cladding could generate intermetallic compounds, high residual stresses, cracks, and crazing. Prior refractory high-entropy-alloy studies reported improved hardness and wear resistance, but the broader requirements of compositional homogeneity, strong bonding, mechanical stability, and preservation of TC4’s beneficial properties remain. Formulate one neutral, testable hypothesis for an intervention that could satisfy these requirements. Specify the intervention, proposed mechanism, predicted outcome relative to untreated TC4, operating or test boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled experiment with an explicit result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Active screen ion nitriding of TC4 at 550°C for 10 hours, under a controlled nitrogen atmosphere at 0.5 atm with real-time process monitoring, will produce a graded nitride layer (outer δ-TiN/ϵ-Ti2N and inner α-Ti(N)) that increases surface hardness by 2–3× and lowers the friction coefficient by roughly 20–30% compared to untreated TC4.
generation.material_initial_state: TC4 (Ti6Al4V) substrate exhibiting a dual-phase α+β microstructure with low surface hardness (~310 HV) and high wear under friction conditions.
generation.intervention: Perform active screen ion nitriding at 550°C for 10 hours in a controlled atmosphere with a nitrogen partial pressure of approximately 0.5 atm, using an active screen and real-time optical emission spectroscopy to maintain consistent process parameters.
generation.conditions: Temperature maintained at 550°C ±10°C, nitriding duration fixed at 10 hours, nitrogen partial pressure stabilized at ~0.5 atm, and continuous monitoring of the plasma environment to ensure uniform ion diffusion.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a graded surface layer characterized by an outer composite nitride region (δ-TiN/ϵ-Ti2N) and an underlying α-Ti(N) diffusion zone with a seamless metallurgical bond to the substrate.
generation.mechanism: Enhanced nitrogen diffusion under controlled conditions leads to the formation of hard interstitial nitride phases at the surface, reducing plastic deformation and contact area while smoothing frictional interactions.
generation.predicted_outcome: The treated TC4 surface will exhibit a hardness increase from ~310 HV to between 620 and 930 HV and a friction coefficient reduction of approximately 20–30% compared to untreated TC4.
generation.baseline: Untreated TC4 alloy with a microhardness of ~310 HV and relatively high friction and wear during sliding contact.
generation.boundary: Effective under laboratory friction and wear testing; deviations in temperature, duration, or nitrogen pressure may lead to nonuniform layer thickness or phase formation.
generation.uncertainty: Uniform nitriding across complex geometries remains challenging; process optimization may be required to avoid over-nitriding or insufficient diffusion in regions with variable heat dissipation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare TC4 samples using the specified active screen ion nitriding process and compare them with untreated samples. Use cross-sectional hardness mapping, X-ray diffraction for phase analysis, and standard pin-on-disc tribological tests.
measurements: Nanoindentation hardness profile across the nitrided layer
XRD to verify the formation of δ-TiN, ϵ-Ti2N, and α-Ti(N) phases
Friction coefficient and wear volume measurements under controlled sliding conditions
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the treated samples fail to show a graded structure with the targeted phases, do not achieve a 2–3× increase in hardness, or do not demonstrate a ~20–30% reduction in friction coefficient relative to untreated TC4, then the hypothesis is refuted.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractThe study assessed the effect of ion nitriding on the properties of the surface layer of Grade 5 titanium alloy used, among others, in medicine. Titanium and its alloys have low hardness and insufficient wear resistance in conditions of friction which limits the use of these materials. The improvement of these properties is only possible by the appropriate modification of the surface layer of these alloys. The ion nitriding process was carried out in a wide temperature range, i.e., 530–590 °C, and in the time range 5–17 h. Two variants of nitriding were applied: cathodic (conventional) nitriding and nitriding using the active screen method. The research results presented in this article allow for stating that each of the applied nitriding variants improves the analysed properties (nitrogen diffusion depth, hardness, wear resistance, microstructure analysis and surface topography) of the surface layers in relation to the material before nitriding. The hardness increased in every nitriding variant (the use of the additional active screen increased the hardness to 1021 HK0.025). The present results depict the preponderant role of temperature on both the structure and the mechanical behavior of the surface layers obtained during PBII surface treatments of Ti-6Al-4V titanium alloy. Whatever the studied temperature, the PBII nitriding process resulted in the formation of two nitride domains. The most superficial one is a “composite” organization of δ-TiN/ϵ-Ti2N, while at depth an α-Ti(N) solid solution is formed. At the lowest studied temperatures (500 °C–700 °C), the response of these two domains to a nanoindentation test presents a continuous evolution of the property gradient with a strong hardening of the surface. The in-depth α-Ti(N) domain presents an increase of hardness with nitrogen insertion into the α-Ti structure, while much stronger changes are observed at the extreme surface, where a δ-TiN/ϵ-Ti2N composite is formed. The α-Ti(N) is expected to prevent the hard and fragile nitride surface layer from breaking (the eggshell effect). At 800 °C, the diffusion process becomes more efficient and leads to a plateau of medium hardness and a smooth mechanical properties gradient in the diffusion layer. papers.title: Corrosion Behavior of TiMoNbX (X = Ta, Cr, Zr) Refractory High Entropy Alloy Coating Prepared by Laser Cladding Based on TC4 Titanium Alloy.
papers.system: TC4 (Ti6Al4V) substrate coated with a refractory high entropy alloy (RHEA)
papers.approach: Laser cladding to deposit RHEA coatings, comparing different alloy compositions (e.g., TiZrAlNb vs. TiZrAlNbCo); focus on microstructure and corrosion behavior.
papers.findings: The TiZrAlNbCo coating showed a fine dendritic structure with a BCC-fcc matrix, and exhibited superior corrosion resistance (Icorr around 3.66 × 10−9 A/cm²) compared to the substrate and TiZrAlNb coating. The presence of an FCC phase was identified as key to microstructural refinement and improved performance.
papers.mechanism: Improved corrosion resistance attributed to the formation of a mixed BCC-fcc structure that refines the microstructure and optimizes phase distributions.

papers.title: Microstructure and Wear Resistance of Si-TC4 Composite Coatings by High-Speed Wire-Powder Laser Cladding.
papers.system: TC4 alloy modified with a composite coating reinforced by in situ formed intermetallics (notably Ti5Si3) from Si addition
papers.approach: High-speed wire–powder laser cladding depositing TC4 wire with concurrently fed Si powders; varied Si feeding rates to control microstructure evolution.
papers.findings: The coating’s microstructure evolved from dendritic to petal, bar, and block shapes with increasing Si powder feed rate; hardness increased significantly (average hardness reaching up to ~909 HV0.2 at optimal feeding rates) and wear resistance was improved, with an optimum at specific Si-feeding conditions.
papers.mechanism: In situ reaction between Si and Ti promotes formation of reinforcing phases (e.g., Ti5Si3) which act as a load-bearing skeleton to improve hardness and wear performance.

papers.title: Effects of Plasma ZrN Metallurgy and Shot Peening Duplex Treatment on Fretting Wear and Fretting Fatigue Behavior of Ti6Al4V Alloy.
papers.system: TC4 alloy with surface modification via a zirconium nitride (ZrN) metallurgical layer and post-treatment shot peening
papers.approach: Glow discharge-based ZrN deposition followed by shot peening; evaluation of fretting wear (FW) and fretting fatigue (FF) under varying slipping amplitudes.
papers.findings: The ZrN layer increased surface hardness and lowered friction; shot peening further enhanced compressive residual stresses. Combined treatment improved FW and, to an extent, FF resistance particularly under high-slipping conditions.
papers.mechanism: Increased hardness from the ZrN phases, lower friction coefficient, combined with induced compressive residual stresses by shot peening, collectively reduce abrasive, oxidation, adhesive, and fatigue wear mechanisms.

papers.title: Microstructure and Wear Behavior of Ti-xFe-SiC In Situ Composite Ceramic Coatings on TC4 Substrate from Laser Cladding.
papers.system: TC4 alloy with an in situ synthesized composite ceramic coating incorporating SiC and Fe modifications
papers.approach: Laser cladding with a two-layer gradient structure – a transition layer to lower dilution (Ti-40SiC) followed by a working layer with varying Fe-content and high-volume-fraction SiC
papers.findings: The coatings achieved up to fivefold increase in hardness (e.g., WL-F15 reached ~1842.9 HV1) relative to the substrate; wear loss was dramatically reduced. Phase analysis showed formation of TiC, Ti5Si3, and Ti3SiC2, with new phases (e.g., TiFeSi2) appearing with higher Fe additions.
papers.mechanism: Fe addition controls the in situ reaction in the Ti-Si-C system, promoting the formation of hard ceramic phases that serve as an interconnected reinforcement network, thereby significantly improving wear resistance.

papers.title: The Influence of Adding B4C and CeO2 on the Mechanical Properties of Laser Cladding Nickel-Based Coatings on the Surface of TC4
papers.system: TC4 alloy coated with Ni-based composite coatings enhanced by additions of B4C and CeO2
papers.approach: Laser cladding using mixtures (Ni60-Ti-Cu) with varying B4C and CeO2 contents to synthesize in situ ceramic reinforcing phases; assessment of microstructure, hardness, friction, and wear performance.
papers.findings: An 8 wt.% B4C addition maximized hardness (up to ~1078 HV) and reduced friction coefficient by ~24.7% relative to TC4; a 3 wt.% CeO2 addition further reduced friction (33.7% lower) and decreased wear volume significantly. The coatings demonstrated improved load-bearing and bonding characteristics.
papers.mechanism: B4C promotes formation of hard phases (e.g., TiC, TiB) with thermal expansion and density matched to TC4, while CeO2 acts as a grain refiner and porosity reducer, leading to enhanced mechanical homogeneity and improved friction/wear properties.

papers.title: Fabrication of a Low Adhesive Superhydrophobic Surface on Ti6Al4V Alloys Using TiO₂/Ni Composite Electrodeposition.
papers.system: TC4 alloy surface modified via composite electrodeposition (TiO₂/Ni) followed by surface chemical modification (FAS)
papers.approach: Composite electrodeposition to build hierarchical micro/nano structures followed by fluoroalkyl silane (FAS) treatment to impart superhydrophobicity
papers.findings: The treated surface achieved a water contact angle of 162.6° and a sliding angle of 1.8°; microhardness nearly doubled (from 310 HV to 587 HV) and friction coefficient dropped from 0.6 to 0.45, with significant wear resistance and mechanical stability evidenced by abrasion tests.
papers.mechanism: Hierarchical structuring reduces effective contact area and traps wear debris, while the chemical modification minimizes adhesion; the composite electrodeposited layer enhances hardness and load distribution.

papers.title: Microstructural and Performance Analysis of (TiAl)₉₅₋ₓCu₅Niₓ Coatings Prepared via Laser Surface Cladding on Ti-6Al-4V
papers.system: TC4 alloy with (TiAl)₉₅₋ₓCu₅Niₓ coatings of varying Ni content
papers.approach: Laser surface cladding with adjustment of Ni content (0, 3, 6, and 9 at.%); detailed study of microstructure, hardness, wear, and tensile behavior
papers.findings: Enhanced hardness and improved wear resistance were observed, with a maximum hardness of ~627.5 HV0.2 at optimum Ni levels (around 6 at.%); tensile strength showed a non-monotonic trend, reflecting a balance between solid solution strengthening and potential embrittlement.
papers.mechanism: Ni incorporation enhances solid solution strengthening within the Ti(Al, Cu)₂ phase, leading to lattice stress that hinders dislocation motion and refines the grain structure.

papers.title: The Effectiveness of Active Screen Method in Ion Nitriding Grade 5 Titanium Alloy.
papers.system: Grade 5 titanium alloy (similar to TC4) undergoing ion nitriding
papers.approach: Ion nitriding conducted with and without an active screen, across a range of temperatures (530–590 °C) and durations (5–17 h)
papers.findings: Both conventional and active screen ion nitriding improved surface hardness and wear resistance, with the active screen variant achieving hardness up to 1021 HK0.025 and significantly reduced abrasion rates, as well as deeper nitrogen diffusion profiles.
papers.mechanism: Enhanced nitrogen diffusion and the formation of a dual nitride structure (a δ-TiN/ϵ-Ti₂N composite domain at the surface and an α-Ti(N) diffusion zone) lead to a graded hardness profile that resists abrasive wear.

papers.title: Study on Surface Integrity and Fatigue Properties of TC4 Titanium Alloy by Surface Ultrasonic Rolling.
papers.system: TC4 alloy treated via surface ultrasonic rolling (SUR)
papers.approach: Application of surface ultrasonic rolling with varied static pressures, feed rates, and rotational speeds; evaluation of changes in surface roughness, hardness, residual stresses, microstructure, and fatigue behavior
papers.findings: Surface roughness was significantly reduced (Ra down to 0.052 μm), microhardness increased by ~35%, and residual compressive stresses were enhanced (from −260 MPa to −685 MPa). Fatigue strength improved markedly (e.g., a 52% increase and fatigue life up to ~7.7 times that of untreated samples).
papers.mechanism: The mechanical working from ultrasonic rolling induces grain refinement, increases dislocation density, and generates compressive residual stresses that collectively improve surface integrity and fatigue resistance.

papers.title: Microstructure and Properties of Ti-Al Coating on Titanium Alloy Surface Assisted by Electromagnetic Field.
papers.system: Titanium alloy surface (TA15) coated with Ti-Al intermetallics (relevant by analogy to TC4 modifications)
papers.approach: Preparation of a Ti-Al coating with and without the assistance of an alternating electromagnetic field to promote alloying and microstructural homogeneity
papers.findings: Application of an electromagnetic field refined the grains, reduced defects, and moderately improved the microhardness of the coating compared to samples processed without the field.
papers.mechanism: Electromagnetic stirring facilitates homogenized mixing, reduces porosity, and refines microstructural features, thereby enhancing mechanical properties.

papers.title: Microstructure, Wear Resistance and Oxidation Behavior of Ni-Ti-Si Coatings Fabricated on Ti6Al4V by Laser Cladding.
papers.system: TC4 alloy with Ni-Ti-Si composite coatings
papers.approach: Laser cladding to deposit coatings incorporating multiple reinforcing phases (e.g., CoTi, TiC, TiB2, Ti5Si3) aimed at enhancing hardness, wear resistance, and oxidation stability
papers.findings: Coatings demonstrated hardness enhancements of 3–4 times over the substrate and significant reductions in wear mass loss, attributed to the formation of a complex composite microstructure.
papers.mechanism: The in situ reaction during laser cladding produces hard phases that act synergistically with the ductile matrix to resist abrasive and adhesive wear.

papers.title: Improving the abrasion resistance of Ti6Al4V alloy by modifying its surface with a diazonium salt and attaching of polyurethane.
papers.system: TC4 alloy surface chemically modified with diazonium salts and overcoated with polyurethane
papers.approach: Surface modification using various diazonium salts to improve adhesion followed by deposition of multiple layers of polyurethane, with characterization via Raman mapping and nanoindentation
papers.findings: The modified alloy exhibited a nearly 10-fold reduction in friction coefficient compared to the untreated alloy and showed excellent stability in simulated body fluids, indicating potential for biomedical applications.
papers.mechanism: The diazonium salt treatment produces reactive surface species that enhance covalent bonding to the polyurethane, yielding a uniform, adherent, and low-friction protective layer.

papers.title: Characteristics of the Structure, Mechanical, and Tribological Properties of a Mo-Mo₂N Nanocomposite Coating Deposited on the Ti6Al4V Alloy
papers.system: TC4 alloy with a Mo-Mo₂N nanocomposite coating
papers.approach: Deposition of a nanocomposite coating containing Mo and Mo₂N phases onto TC4, followed by tribological evaluation
papers.findings: The coating exhibited enhanced hardness and improved tribological properties including reduced wear, attributed to the unique nanocomposite structure.
papers.mechanism: The nanocomposite architecture provides a high density of hard, wear-resistant phases that enhance load distribution and reduce wear-induced damage.

papers.title: Microstructure and Wear Resistance of Ti6Al4V Titanium Alloy Laser-Clad Ni60/WC Composite Coating.
papers.system: TC4 alloy with Ni60/WC composite coating
papers.approach: Laser cladding Ni60 mixed with 35% WC onto TC4 with varied laser scanning speeds to optimize phase composition, microstructure, and tribological performance
papers.findings: At optimal scanning speeds, the coatings achieved significant improvements in hardness and wear resistance, linked to the formation of reinforced phases and a strong metallurgical bond.
papers.mechanism: WC additions contribute hard particles that improve wear resistance and overall surface hardness while preserving the bonding integrity with the substrate.

papers.title: Microstructure and Wear Resistance of In Situ Synthesized Ti(C, N) Ceramic-Reinforced Nickel-Based Coatings by Laser Cladding.
papers.system: TC4 alloy with a nickel-based coating in which Ti(C,N) ceramics are synthesized in situ
papers.approach: Laser cladding with a powder blend containing TiN, pure Ti, graphite, and In625 to induce decomposition of TiN and formation of Ti(C,N) phases within a nickel matrix
papers.findings: At higher powder addition levels (e.g., 40%), the coating showed a reduced friction coefficient (approx. 0.829× that of the substrate) and a wear volume only 0.145× that of the substrate, owing to an increased volume fraction of hard ceramic phases.
papers.mechanism: In situ formation of TiC, Ti(C,N), and related hard phases creates a backbone structure that resists micro-cutting and adhesive wear by impeding crack propagation and debris movement.

papers.title: Surface Alloying and Improved Property of Nb on TC4 Induced by High Current Pulsed Electron Beam.
papers.system: TC4 alloy surface modified via Nb alloying
papers.approach: High current pulsed electron beam (HCPEB) treatment to alloy Nb onto the TC4 surface
papers.findings: Nb was successfully dissolved into the TC4 matrix, enhancing the passivation tendency and improving corrosion resistance without compromising other mechanical properties.
papers.mechanism: Nb alloying induces solid solution effects that refine the surface microstructure and improve the corrosion and possibly wear performance through enhanced passivation.

papers.title: Tribological Properties of Ti6Al4V Alloy Composite Texture Fabricated by Ultrasonic Strengthening Grinding and Laser Processing.
papers.system: TC4 alloy with a composite surface texture created by a combination of ultrasonic strengthening grinding and laser texturing
papers.approach: Process combining ultrasonic strengthening grinding (USGP) to form a fine-grained, high-hardness surface, followed by laser processing to introduce textured features
papers.findings: The composite texture reduced effective contact area, trapped wear debris, and led to improved load distribution which in turn reduced abrasive wear and enhanced overall tribological performance.
papers.mechanism: The hierarchical, textured surface structure minimizes three-body abrasive wear while the underlying strengthened layer (via grain refinement and high dislocation density) provides enhanced load-bearing capacity.

established: TC4 (Ti6Al4V) alloys possess inherently low hardness and poor wear resistance which limits their performance in high-contact-stress or extreme service conditions.

Surface modification techniques can improve wear resistance and hardness by creating reinforced layers, inducing compressive residual stresses, and forming in situ hard phases without altering the advantageous properties of the bulk alloy.
Strong metallurgical bonding and compositional homogeneity between the coating and substrate are crucial for preserving the mechanical integrity of TC4.

approaches_tried.outcome: Produced weak coatings with poor substrate bonding
Suffered from uneven constituent dispersion and weak interfaces

approaches_tried.approach: Laser cladding (with various additives such as Si, B4C, CeO₂, Ni-based mixtures, and refractory high entropy alloys)
approaches_tried.outcome: Improved hardness and wear resistance in many cases, but issues such as formation of brittle intermetallic phases, high residual stresses, and occasional cracking were observed
Enhanced nitrogen diffusion and formation of graded nitride layers resulted in increased hardness and wear resistance
Reduced surface roughness, increased hardness and compressive residual stress, and significantly improved fatigue life

approaches_tried.approach: Plasma ZrN metallurgy with shot peening
approaches_tried.outcome: Improved fretting wear resistance by combining a hard ZrN layer with compressive residual stresses from shot peening

approaches_tried.approach: Composite electrodeposition to achieve superhydrophobic, low friction surfaces
approaches_tried.outcome: Formation of hierarchical structures yielding very low adhesive friction and increased wear resistance
Improved corrosion resistance and potentially enhanced surface properties through Nb solid-solution formation

approaches_tried.approach: Ultrasonic strengthening grinding combined with laser processing for texture formation
approaches_tried.outcome: Enhanced tribological performance through reduced contact area and improved debris management

approaches_tried.approach: Surface chemical modification followed by polymer coating
approaches_tried.outcome: Achieved extremely low friction coefficients and stable abrasion resistance suitable for biomedical implant applications

mechanisms: In situ formation of hard phases (e.g., TiC, Ti5Si3, Ti(C,N), TiB, TiN) reinforces the coating and increases hardness.
Grain refinement and formation of a fine, homogeneous microstructure improve load distribution and wear resistance.
Induction of compressive residual stresses (via shot peening, ultrasonic rolling or nitriding) enhances fatigue and abrasion resistance.
Solid solution strengthening (e.g., via Ni or Nb alloying) adjusts lattice parameters and hinders dislocation motion.
Hierarchical and textured surface structures reduce effective contact area and trap wear debris, thereby reducing three-body abrasive wear.
disagreements: While laser cladding improves hardness and wear resistance, some studies report problems such as high residual stresses, formation of brittle intermetallic compounds, and cracking that may compromise ductility.

There is variation in optimal additive contents (e.g., different percentages for Si, B4C, CeO₂, Ni) and process parameters among studies, suggesting a lack of consensus on achieving uniformly optimal performance.
Some methods (e.g., plasma ZrN with shot peening) may improve fretting wear resistance but at the potential cost of reduced fatigue resistance of the base material.
open_questions: How can a coating/intervention be designed to simultaneously achieve high hardness, superior wear resistance, strong substrate bonding, and preservation of TC4’s intrinsic properties under extreme conditions?
What are the optimal combinations of process parameters and additive contents to control phase formation and residual stress during laser cladding?
Can hybrid techniques (e.g., combining ion nitriding with in situ composite synthesis) overcome the drawbacks observed with individual surface modification methods?
What are the long-term stability and performance of these modified surfaces under real extreme-service and high-contact-stress conditions?
opportunities: Exploring hybrid processes that combine the benefits of ion nitriding (or active screen methods) with laser cladding to produce graded, compositionally homogeneous, and strongly bonded coatings.
Optimizing the additive composition (e.g., combining B4C with rare earth oxides or Nb alloying via HCPEB) to achieve a balanced formation of hard phases and ductile matrix properties.
Leveraging processes that induce beneficial compressive residual stresses (e.g., shot peening or ultrasonic rolling) alongside in situ ceramic formation to address wear and fatigue simultaneously.

Investigating composite structures with engineered hierarchical textures (using techniques such as ultrasonic strengthening grinding plus laser processing) for improved debris management and contact mechanics under high load conditions.

directions.direction: Laser cladding of a Ni60‐based composite coating with controlled additions of B4C and CeO2
directions.assessment: This approach directly targets the low hardness and poor wear resistance by in situ formation of hard ceramic phases with strong metallurgical bonding. It is supported by evidence showing that optimized B4C and CeO2 additions can yield coatings with 3–3.5× increased hardness and friction reductions of 25–35% compared to TC4, while maintaining substrate integrity [PMC11313005::web::004::1_introduction, PMC11313005::web::016::3_1_3_friction_and_wear_property]. The physics and phase‐formation mechanisms are well understood, though potential brittleness must be monitored.

directions.direction: Active screen ion nitriding of TC4 to create graded nitride layers
directions.assessment: Ion nitriding using an active screen produces a dual-domain structure (a superficial δ-TiN/ϵ-Ti2N composite and an underlying α-Ti(N) diffusion zone) that enhances surface hardness and wear resistance without altering the substrate core properties. This method preserves the alloy's beneficial ductility while improving surface performance and is backed by quantitative studies [PMC8304058::web::000::abstract, PMC9785563::web::014::4_conclusions]. The process parameters (temperature and time) are tunable, making it highly feasible.

directions.direction: Plasma ZrN metallurgy combined with post-shot peening
directions.type: Surface or Coating Modification Coupled with Mechanical Treatment
directions.assessment: This combined approach first deposits a thin, hard ZrN layer via plasma metallurgy and then introduces beneficial compressive stresses by shot peening. It improves both abrasion and fretting wear properties by increasing hardness (to near 1700 HK) and residual compressive stress while maintaining a strong metallurgical bond with the substrate [PMC5502668::web::014::3_5_fw_behavior, PMC5502668::web::020::4_discussion]. It directly addresses high-contact-stress performance, though the interplay between hardness and toughness requires careful control.

directions.direction: Composite electrodeposition of TiO2/Ni followed by FAS chemical modification
directions.type: Surface Modification via Low-Temperature Deposition and Chemical Treatment
directions.assessment: This approach employs composite electrodeposition to generate hierarchical micro/nano structures on TC4, which are then chemically modified with FAS to impart superhydrophobicity and reduce friction. It doubles surface hardness and reduces friction coefficients significantly (up to ~25–30%), offering a low-temperature process that preserves the bulk properties of TC4. Prior work supports its feasibility and mechanical stability under simulated wear conditions [PMC6413079::web::028::4_conclusions].

needs: Empirical data on typical hardness values of plasma-deposited ZrN plus residual stress levels that have been independently measured for Ti6Al4V to confirm the target range is feasible.
Studies comparing the effect of shot-peening conditions on the formation and stability of compressive stress in ZrN-coated TC4.
Experimental data or references supporting the claim that the proposed ZrN layer and shot peening can achieve the predicted hardness and wear resistance without causing surface embrittlement.
Studies demonstrating the long-term stability and adhesion of ZrN coatings under cyclic loading conditions.

The hypothesis assumes that the shot peening process will achieve uniform compressive residual stresses of -600 MPa without causing surface embrittlement, which is not guaranteed and requires further validation.

Further studies on the effects of shot peening on the residual stress state and wear resistance of ZrN coatings, particularly in relation to the optimization of shot peening parameters and the potential effects on coating properties.
Published test results correlating ion nitriding parameters (time, temperature, environment) with thickness and uniformity of δ-TiN/ϵ-Ti2N layers.
Comparative tribology data showing friction reductions near 20–30% for active-screen nitrided Ti6Al4V from multiple sources.
Additional data or references confirming the ability of active screen ion nitriding to produce a graded nitride layer with the proposed hardness and friction reduction.
Studies on the long-term stability and wear resistance of similar nitrided layers under high-contact stress conditions.

Further studies on the effects of active screen ion nitriding on the microstructure and properties of TC4 alloys, particularly in relation to the optimization of nitriding parameters and coating thickness uniformity.

candidates.hypothesis: A Ni60-Ti-Cu composite coating with 8 wt.% B4C and 3 wt.% CeO2 applied via laser cladding will form in situ hard ceramic phases (e.g., TiC and TiB) that increase the surface hardness of TC4 by approximately 3.5 times and reduce the friction coefficient by 25–35% compared to untreated TC4.
candidates.intervention: Laser cladding deposition of a Ni60-Ti-Cu-based composite powder mix containing 8 wt.% B4C and 3 wt.% CeO2.

candidates.hypothesis: Active screen ion nitriding of TC4 at 550°C for 10 hours will produce a graded nitride layer with an outer δ-TiN/ϵ-Ti2N composite and an underlying α-Ti(N) diffusion zone that increases surface hardness by approximately 2–3 times and lowers the friction coefficient compared to untreated TC4.
candidates.intervention: Perform active screen ion nitriding at a temperature of 550°C for 10 hours under a controlled nitrogen atmosphere with an activated screen.

candidates.hypothesis: Plasma deposition of an 8-μm-thick ZrN layer on TC4 followed by shot peening to induce compressive residual stresses up to -600 MPa will result in a surface with microhardness exceeding 1700 HK and enhanced wear resistance under high-contact stress conditions relative to untreated TC4.
candidates.intervention: Apply plasma ZrN metallurgy to deposit an ~8-μm thick ZrN layer on TC4, then perform shot peening with configured parameters to induce compressive residual stresses.

candidates.hypothesis: Composite electrodeposition of a TiO2/Ni layer followed by FAS modification on TC4 will create a hierarchical micro/nano structured surface that doubles the microhardness (from ~310 HV to ~580 HV) and reduces the friction coefficient by approximately 25–30% relative to untreated TC4 while maintaining excellent substrate adhesion.
candidates.intervention: Perform composite electrodeposition to deposit a TiO2/Ni layer onto TC4, then chemically modify the surface with fluoroalkyl silane (FAS) to impart superhydrophobicity and lower adhesion.

candidates.hypothesis: Plasma deposition of an 8-μm-thick ZrN layer on TC4 followed by shot peening to induce compressive residual stresses up to -600 MPa will result in a surface with microhardness exceeding 1700 HK and enhanced wear resistance under high-contact stress conditions relative to untreated TC4.
candidates.intervention: Apply plasma ZrN metallurgy to deposit an ~8-μm thick ZrN layer on TC4, then perform shot peening with configured parameters to induce compressive residual stresses.

candidates.hypothesis: Active screen ion nitriding of TC4 at 550°C for 10 hours, under a controlled nitrogen atmosphere at 0.5 atm with real-time process monitoring, will produce a graded nitride layer (outer δ-TiN/ϵ-Ti2N and inner α-Ti(N)) that increases surface hardness by 2–3× and lowers the friction coefficient by roughly 20–30% compared to untreated TC4.
candidates.intervention: Perform active screen ion nitriding at 550°C for 10 hours in a controlled atmosphere with a nitrogen partial pressure of approximately 0.5 atm, using an active screen and real-time optical emission spectroscopy to maintain consistent process parameters.
candidates.changes: Added specific details on nitrogen partial pressure control, real‐time monitoring for uniform nitriding, and clarified strategies to mitigate over‐ or under‐nitriding based on reviewer feedback.

candidates.hypothesis: Composite electrodeposition of a TiO2/Ni layer onto TC4 at a current density of 5 mA/cm² for 20 minutes, followed by immersion in a 1% FAS solution at room temperature for 30 minutes, will yield a hierarchical micro/nano structure that doubles the microhardness from ~310 HV to ~580 HV and reduces the friction coefficient by roughly 25–30% while ensuring excellent substrate adhesion.
candidates.intervention: Conduct composite electrodeposition using an electrolyte containing dispersed TiO2 nanoparticles and Ni salts at a current density of 5 mA/cm² for 20 minutes, then perform FAS chemical modification by immersing the samples in a 1% fluoroalkyl silane solution at ambient temperature for 30 minutes.
candidates.changes: Specified electrodeposition parameters and FAS treatment conditions, and addressed concerns about adhesion and durability under cyclic loading by clarifying process parameters.

candidates.hypothesis: A Ni60-Ti-Cu composite coating with 8 wt.% B4C and 3 wt.% CeO2 applied via laser cladding—using optimized parameters (e.g., laser power 1.5 kW, scanning speed 12 mm/s, powder feed rate 10 g/min under argon)—will in situ form hard ceramic phases (such as TiC and TiB) that increase surface hardness by approximately 3.5× (from ~310 HV to ~1070–1100 HV) and reduce the friction coefficient by 25–35% compared to untreated TC4.
candidates.intervention: Laser cladding deposition of a Ni60-Ti-Cu-based powder blend containing 8 wt.% B4C and 3 wt.% CeO2, using a laser cladding system with specified parameters (1.5 kW power, 12 mm/s scan speed, and 10 g/min powder feed) under an inert argon atmosphere.
candidates.changes: Included precise laser cladding parameters and a discussion of process optimization to control residual stresses and avoid brittle intermetallic formation.

candidates.hypothesis: Plasma deposition of an ~8-μm-thick ZrN layer on TC4 followed by shot peening (using 0.5 mm diameter shots at an Almen intensity of 8 with 150% coverage) to induce compressive residual stresses up to -600 MPa will yield a surface with microhardness exceeding 1700 HK and enhanced wear resistance under high-contact stress conditions compared to untreated TC4.
candidates.intervention: Apply plasma ZrN metallurgy to deposit an ~8-μm thick ZrN layer on the TC4 substrate using controlled gas flow and power settings, followed by shot peening using 0.5 mm diameter shots at an Almen intensity of 8 and 150% surface coverage.
candidates.changes: Specified plasma deposition and shot peening parameters, and added discussion to avoid surface embrittlement while achieving the target compressive stress, based on reviewer feedback.
